itinerary.cal: The Mildred Lakes trailhead sits at the end of FR-25 off the Hamma Hamma River road; check Olympic National Forest alerts before going, as this area has been affected by wildfire closures in recent years.

days.note: The Mildred Lakes Trail is unmaintained and notoriously rough - steep root/rock ladders requiring hands and feet, especially past Huckleberry Creek - so most parties treat it as a half-day in with a full overnight pack. Camp in the Mildred Lakes basin below Sawtooth Ridge, which also serves as the base for nearby Mount Cruiser and Mount Stone.
days.title: Backpack in to Mildred Lakes camp
days.objective: Set up basecamp near Mildred Lakes

days.note: An early start lets you cache overnight gear at camp and climb light: scramble talus and side-hill terrain up toward the summit ridge, then a short class 2-3 section (rock is notoriously rotten) to the top. After descending to camp, break camp and hike the brutal trail back out the same afternoon - a long but standard weekend pattern for this approach.
days.title: Summit push and hike out

schedule.label: Alpine start from camp
schedule.detail: Light daypacks, overnight gear cached at camp.

schedule.label: Reach base of summit scramble terrain
schedule.detail: Talus, side-hilling, and contouring below the summit ridge on loose, rotten rock.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Class 2-3 finish; take care on the rotten rock near the top.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Down-climb the summit section carefully, then break camp and re-pack for the hike out.

schedule.detail: Full overnight pack back down the steep, rooted Mildred Lakes trail.

days.objective: Climb Mount Skokomish (6,434 ft) and return to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day, 1-night weekend trip: roughly 13 miles round trip with about 5,300 ft of cumulative gain, most parties backpacking in on day one and combining the summit push with the full hike-out on day two.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at Mildred Lakes and Putvin trailheads (no fee at the trailhead itself otherwise). Entering via Staircase/Olympic NP requires the $30 park entrance fee (7-day private-vehicle pass; $15 for a walk-in/bike individual pass) or an interagency pass, plus an $8 per person per night backcountry camping fee (booked via Recreation.gov) for Flapjack Lakes.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness regulations apply (no bikes/motorized use, max group size limits, camp 200 ft from water). Mountain goats are frequently encountered around the peak's base and Lake of the Angels basin — do not approach or feed them; give them a wide berth as they can be aggressive toward hikers seeking salt.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required on Olympic National Forest land (Mildred Lakes, Putvin). If approaching via Flapjack Lakes inside Olympic National Park, an overnight wilderness camping permit is required, reservable on Recreation.gov for the Flapjack Lakes zone (bookable mid-April, camping dates mid-June through mid-October); contact the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.
access.closures: UPDATED (as of July 8, 2026): the Mildred Lakes Trail (#822) and Mildred Lakes Trailhead on FS-25 — along with the Mt. Rose Trail/Trailhead, Dry Creek East Trailhead, and the Staircase developed area (campground, ranger station, Rapids Loop Trail) — REOPENED on July 8, 2026 per a joint Olympic National Forest/Olympic National Park press release, ending the closure tied to the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire. Still CLOSED pending hazard-tree removal and infrastructure repair: wilderness trails beyond the developed Staircase area, including the North Fork Skokomish River Trail (from the Staircase Rapids Loop to Home Sweet Home) and the Flapjack Lakes Trail, plus FS-2451 and the Copper Creek Trail. The Putvin Trail/Lake of the Angels approach, on a different drainage further north off Hamma Hamma River Road, was never part of this closure and remains the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. Always check the Olympic National Forest alerts page and NPS Olympic fire-conditions page before a trip, as backcountry trail status keeps changing as repair work continues through summer 2026.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District) for the Mildred Lakes and Putvin trailheads; Olympic National Park (Wilderness Information Center) for the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish/Flapjack Lakes side.
access.land_manager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: None for day use; NPS wilderness permit for overnight camping.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit
overnight_permit.where: Get it in advance on Recreation.gov, by phone, or in person at a park Wilderness Information Center. Upper Lena Lake is quota-limited, so book early for July to September.

before.overview: A rugged, three-summited peak (south summit is highest) in the southeastern Olympics within the Mount Skokomish Wilderness, straddling the Olympic National Park boundary near Mount Stone. Built of rotten Eocene pillow basalt, it is reached by a tough, largely off-trail approach and a loose Class 2-3 scramble to the broad summit block. Access to this specific approach (Mildred Lakes / Flapjack Lakes) is currently closed by a Forest Service/NPS order tied to the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent on all approaches once off Hamma Hamma River Road/FS-25; the Mildred Lakes and Staircase/Flapjack approaches are inside the active Bear Gulch Fire closure area, so parties attempting those lines are trespassing on a closed trail in addition to the terrain hazards.

before.approach: The standard-route trailhead is the Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of Hwy 101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft elevation. Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels, not Mildred or Flapjack Lakes - those serve neighboring Mount Cruiser/Mount Lena out of the North Fork Skokomish/Staircase side. From the trailhead, Putvin Trail #812 is unmaintained for its last ~1.6 miles but well-traveled and easy to follow when snow-free; the tread is notably steep and narrow with unstable footing in spots as it climbs through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles in, the trail breaks into the open, grassy Whitehorse Creek basin and continues up to Lake of the Angels (about 3.5 miles and roughly 2,800-3,000 ft of gain from the trailhead, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace), a scenic alpine lake sitting in a cirque below Mount Stone and the Skokomish massif - this is the last reliable water source and the standard camp for an overnight trip. From the lake, climb westerly up pleasant alpine/heather slopes to a broad 5,800-ft saddle at the northeastern end of Mount Skokomish. From the saddle, a boot path/way-trail contours south and southwest across scree, grass, and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn, before turning to climb the final scree/rock slopes to the summit ridge. Total round-trip stats commonly cited are roughly 9-12 miles and about 5,000-5,100 ft of gain, with climbing parties reporting 3.5-5 hours up. Hazards: the narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread; lingering steep snow and real avalanche exposure on the upper slopes well into summer (reports note hazard even in August/September); and notoriously rotten 'Olympic choss' rock and loose scree/talus on the upper mountain and summit block, which is the crux of the route more than any single technical move.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
approach_variants.notes: THIS IS THE STANDARD APPROACH AND THE ROUTE'S WAYPOINT LIST DESCRIBES A DIFFERENT ONE. Published and trip-report accounts are consistent that Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 2,800-3,000 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND AT LAKE OF THE ANGELS AND THE CIRQUE ITSELF TELLS YOU WHICH WAY TO GO: MOUNT STONE IS ON YOUR RIGHT, ANOTHER PEAK IS ON YOUR LEFT, AND MOUNT SKOKOMISH IS STRAIGHT AHEAD. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

THE TURN IS AROUND THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE LAKE, on a way trail heading WEST to the ridge. Then take a broad gully SOUTHWEST and up toward the SADDLE JUST NORTH OF POINT 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud, which is why it is quoted here rather than a description of the terrain.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours SOUTH and SOUTHWEST across scree, grass and rock benches around the EAST and SOUTH flanks of the peak, PASSING A LARGE TARN. The tarn is the confirmation. TURN RIGHT AND START CLIMBING WHEN YOU ARE ABOVE THE LARGE TARN — that is the published trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

THIRD TEST, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around LEFT to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has THREE SUMMIT HORNS and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

EXPLICIT WARNING FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is directional: contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut WEST over the ridge instead.

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.notes: RECORDED BECAUSE THE ROUTE'S OWN WAYPOINTS DESCRIBE THIS APPROACH, not because it is the standard one. It is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford HUCKLEBERRY CREEK at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot ROOT AND ROCK LADDERS, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE ON THIS SIDE IS THE OPEN BASIN AND SADDLE BENEATH THE SOUTH PEAK AT ABOUT 5,500 FT, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS UNDERFOOT: THE FOOTING TURNS TO LOOSE, ROTTEN ROCK FROM THERE UP. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. THE TEST FOR THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE ROOT LADDER, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then DESCENDS off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS VARIANT IS SECOND: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. Published and trip-report accounts put the standard route on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

weather.typical: Olympics-influenced maritime weather: wetter, cloudier conditions can linger into early summer before drier, warmer patterns take over July-September
weather.probability: Sudden marine fog or weather changes can roll in with little warning even in summer; afternoon thunderstorms are less common here than in the Cascades but not impossible

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Exposed Class 3 scrambling on loose, rotten Olympic rock near the summit where a fall would be serious given the poor rock quality and remoteness; the steep snow gullies on the approach carry real slip/slide fall risk into early summer and require ice axe and self-arrest competence

avalanche.zone: N/A for non-glaciated terrain, but the summit-saddle gullies carry real wet-slide/sluffing avalanche potential well into the summer climbing season (slides have been reported even in August/September) — assess snow conditions on-site rather than assuming off-season safety

before.descent_text: Two options: walk off to the southwest, contouring around Amphitheatre back to Upper Cathedral Lake camp, or descend via the small col southwest of the North Ridge and down a 3rd-class gully on the north slope.

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning from Cathedral Pass or lake camp

hazards: Long, remote approach with no quick evacuation.
before.turnaround: Even at low technical grade this is a long, loose alpine ridge with no fast retreat — turn around on deteriorating weather rather than pushing through a thunderstorm on an exposed ridge.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage; long rescue response time given remoteness.

climate.fall: Larches gold late Sept-early Oct; snow possible by mid-Oct.
climate.spring: Snowbound into June; possible early-season snow climb variant but unconfirmed by sources.
climate.typical: High, semi-arid east-slope alpine climate; frequent summer afternoon thunderstorms.

before.best_season: Can go earlier in the season than the buttress rock routes since much of it is 3rd-4th class scrambling; late June through September, with July-August most stable.

before.itinerary: Typically combined with Eldorado Peak's East Ridge as a multi-day trip: Day 1 approach to a high camp (~5,700-7,600 ft gain); Day 2 climb Dorado Needle's East Ridge from camp (8-12 hours round trip); Day 3 descend to the trailhead.
before.rappels: Two short rappels from the sub-summit into the notch below the summit pyramid; descent adds further rappels/downclimbing on the Northwest Ridge (or an alternate 2-rappel north-face variant).
before.detailed_rack: Single rack to 3 inches (cams 0.3-3, optional doubles in 0.5-1) with a single 60m rope; ice axe, crampons, and a trekking pole for glacier approach.
before.approach: Access is via Port Angeles up the paved Hurricane Ridge Road (an NPS entrance fee/pass is required), then onto the unpaved, narrow Obstruction Point Road for about 2 miles to a point where the road runs almost directly beneath the formation. Steeple Rock is a roughly 200-foot spire close enough to the road that the walk-up is short, commonly described as around 20 minutes or less depending on which side is approached. It sees light traffic. Because Obstruction Point Road is seasonal and weather-dependent, this approach is realistically only viable roughly mid-July through early October. For this specific route: reach the south-side terrace via the SW spur along the south side of the ridge; Direct Finish is a summit-finish variation from the same terrace.
